title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
summary: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators . Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood. A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms). Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. summary: Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers. Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing. Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress. Using the NVIDIA cu DSS library, multiphysics software provider COMSOL is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically. In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating NVIDIA cu Litho into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print. As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes. title: It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive
summary:
**Core Story / Main Event**

**Key Findings & Scientific Context**  
- Researchers combined climate‑model projections with 650,000 citizen‑science observations from iNaturalist to assess cactus vulnerability.  
- Cacti, though iconic for drought resilience, actually require water and rely on seasonal monsoon rains (often July or August in the southwestern U.S.).  
- Adaptations such as a waxy skin help retain rainwater, but under projected climate conditions cacti become “much, much sicker” than previously thought.  
- Sublethal drought effects include reduced growth, increased mortality, and failure to flower, which can shrink populations over time.  
- In the Sonoran Desert, the iconic saguaro cactus is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts because it does not always flower.  
- Other stressors—habitat loss, poaching, rising sea levels—compound the threat; for example, the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida has gone locally extinct due to excess water from sea‑level rise.  
- Higher nighttime temperatures impair cactus respiration, and when combined with watering, can cause rot.

**Potential Natural Responses**  
- Some cactus populations may shift into areas whose climates more closely match the conditions they evolved under, similar to Arctic plants moving northward in search of suitable weather and water.

**Conservation Implications & Actions**  
- Conservationists can evacuate cacti to botanical gardens where they can be cared for under changing climate conditions.  
- Reintroduction into the wild is possible if drought and high temperatures no longer threaten the population.  
- Governments must protect lands where cacti are threatened; the research can help prioritize these efforts.

title: How much electricity does your home sound system typically use?
summary:
**Core Story / Main Event**  
- The article explains how much electricity a typical home sound system uses, how to think about that usage, and how to measure it accurately.

**Important Names, Companies, Brands, and Key People**  
- Engadget (source of the article)  
- Grassetto/Getty Images (image credit)  
- Nanci Santos/Getty Images (image credit)  
- sommart sombutwanitkul/Shutterstock (image credit)  
- Federal Reserve (source of electricity cost data)

**Key Facts & Figures**  

- **Typical Power Draw**  
  - Standby mode: **20–50 watts**  
  - Maximum volume: **≈200 watts**  

- **Component‑Level Power**  
  - Turntables and CD players: **minimal power**  
  - Volume level: **directly proportional to energy consumption**  
  - Audiophiles with high‑end or vintage analog gear: **higher running costs**  
  - Independently powered speakers: **more energy** than amp‑driven speakers  
  - Large home‑theatre systems: **even higher energy use**  

- **Other Energy‑Consuming Accessories**  
  - Battery‑powered components left plugged in: **degrade cells over time** (modern streaming speakers designed to mitigate this)  
  - USB chargers: **draw power in standby**  

- **Measurement Methodology**  
  1. **List all components** of your system.  
  2. **Identify wattage** and average daily use for each item (consult manuals or manufacturer websites).  
  3. **Use an inexpensive watt meter** (plugged between the device and wall socket) to measure actual power draw.  
  4. **Take readings at both high and low volumes** to capture realistic range.  
  5. **Measure standby consumption** (device on but not in use).  
  6. **Smart plugs**: provide accurate energy data and allow remote switching off to eliminate standby draw.  

- **Energy‑Cost Calculation Formula**  
  - **Daily energy (kWh)** = (Wattage × Time in hours) ÷ 1,000  
  - **Monthly cost** = [Daily kWh × Days per month] × Cost per kWh  

- **Example Calculation**  
  - Device: **100‑watt amplifier**  
  - Usage: **5 hours/day** for **30 days**  
  - Daily energy: (100 W × 5 h) ÷ 1,000 = 0.5 kWh  
  - Monthly energy: 0.5 kWh × 30 = **15 kWh**  
  - Cost per kWh (U.S. current rate): **$0.196**  
  - Monthly cost: 15 kWh × $0.196 = **$2.94**  
  - Annual cost: $2.94 × 12 ≈ **$36**  
  - Comparison: “nearly $36 each year to run, so about the price of a couple of lattes, a nice lunch, or four months of a Netflix subscription.”  

- **Applicability**  
  - The formula works for any electrical device (e.g., smart bulbs vs. LED bulbs).

- None provided in the text.
